rv.q: The century-old play holds up marvelously, and its two leads don’t waste a drop of opportunity for drunken laughs.
If you’re looking for pure escapist fun to provide some immediate relief, “Fallen Angels” can’t be beat.
Broadway has not seen a more delectable diversion this season than the bubbly revival of Noël Coward’s early comedy “Fallen Angels,” starring the glittering duo of Rose Byrne and Kelli O’Hara.
Fallen Angels is a most welcome springtime treat, a smart, breezy entry in Broadway’s chaotically busy pre
Director Scott Ellis understands all this, and thus the admirably specific physical business and slurred verbosity in his gently outré revival really makes for quite the amusing diversion.
In a moment when sublime silliness can, in its very studied triviality, provide a spiritual antidote, they’ve been the best drunk slumber party companions a gal could wish for.

The two are so silly, so loopily in synch, that the scene, which occurs halfway through the second act, lifts the entire show, giving it a buoyancy that has been lacking during its exposition-heavy beginning.
Watching such a fine-china actress as O’Hara shatter on the floor, sliding down designer David Rockwell’s grand staircase and crudely spitting out sweets, is a hoot.
Fallen Angels is an all-around delight, from its starry cast to its exuberant physical comedy and beautiful costumes.
Byrne and O'Hara are the main reasons to see this excellent revival.
Thankfully, O’Hara and Byrne are so wonderful—and so wonderfully matched—that there’s no getting annoyed with either of them.

That's Fallen Angels, an evening of good silly fun, skillfully directed and performed by a cast that is both solid in their delivery and comfortable enough to take on a loosey-goosey style, speak in catch-as-catch-can British accents, and even make each other laugh.

Like the bubbly champagne that's served onstage, 'Fallen Angels' is a perfect pick-me-up.
Byrne, O’Hara and Ellis turn Coward’s champagne bubble of a script into a showcase for comic finesse.
Scott Ellis’ sumptuous staging of this early Coward is highly enjoyable, a sugary bonbon of a production that goes down nice and easy.
She’s the chief reason to see Fallen Angels, the next stage of her decades-long affair with Broadway audiences, alit with a flame that only keeps burning brighter.
Yes, there are traces of the wicked Coward wit, although it’s not as sharp as the playwright’s more frequently produced comedies (Blithe Spirit, Hay Fever, Present Laughter, Private Lives.)

Even at the very un-Coward-like length of 90 minutes, this production of “Fallen Angels” under the direction of Scott Ellis takes about half an hour to light any real comic fire in what was once the play’s first act. Director Scott Ellis tends to rush the pace of the comedy, when taking a bit more leisure about it might make Coward’s already clipped dialogue easier to appreciate. His staging takes surprisingly little advantage of the expansive set and its deluxe furnishings. The program notes that Coward revised...
“Fallen Angels” looks handsome and sounds promising on paper, but in execution, it proves curiously insubstantial, a revival with style to spare but little reason to exist.
I smiled and snickered but a hearty laugh ne’er escaped me.
Thanks to the extravagant characters and the husbands who provide blunt, basic foils, Fallen Angels is a rollicking good time.
New York audiences should cheer that these “Fallen Angels” have successfully landed on Broadway this season.

Mad & Hell, Mame & Vera, Elphaba & Glinda--one can add to this short list of famous frenemies of stage, the names Julia and Jane, the delightful and dastardly dynamic diva duo in the current revival of Noel Coward’s Fallen Angels, played magnificently by Kelli O’Hara and Rose Byrne, respectively.
Rose Byrne and Kelli O’Hara are a champagne-soaked delight.
Chimoo is a scene-swiping treat who brings an uproarious mix of smug self-satisfaction and reluctant deference to the role.
Fallen Angels runs but 90 minutes and while you wish for bigger laughs and more assured style, it'll be over before you feel like sneaking out.
With two heaven-sent actresses, it is unfortunately left to the gifted Rose Byrne and Kelli O’Hara to grapple with a play that has always been a bit of a soufflé and is now downgraded to a trifle.

cn.t: Critics find this Coward revival a fizzy, entertaining showcase for stars Rose Byrne and Kelli O'Hara, who excel in drunken slapstick, though some note the 1925 comedy's material feels thin and the production occasionally lags.

dr.inst: Available through the TodayTix app. Credit card. Limit 2.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
